I would go up on to the deck  of a sailing boat , climb the mast  into the yards  by the rigging , and then go on with my outing in a skiff  among the heavy fishing boats , where the nets  hang drying.
k.t10-17-1: 17. — On the quay  the most varied goods  passed before me, packed in crates  or in bales . They made up the cargo  of the barges, and powerful cranes  lifted them out and set them down on lorries  while the carriers declared them and paid the duty at the customs house .
k.t10-18-1: 18. — At last, when I reached the swing bridge  or the lock , passing the dredger  that cleans out the canal , I would land on the pier beside the signal mast .
k.t10-19-1: 19. — It is on the other side of that pier that the launches  bringing the squadron’s officers ashore come alongside. It is a fine sight to see the sailors raise their oars in time while the boat, carried by the wave , comes easily up to the landing steps. It is here that one can best watch the tide and the movement of the ebb and flow on the beach .
k.t10-20-1: 20. — To get home I took the electric tram , whose stop  is at the post standing in front of the officers’ club.
k.t10-20-2: From the balcony  of the club, decorated with anchors , guns and cannonballs, I often saw a splendid gathering of naval officers: lieutenants  with their swords, captains of artillery  and of infantry  with their sabres. Behind them stood a sailor  who brought them a telescope when they wanted to make out what was happening far off.
k.t10-21-1: 21. — I also saw young sub-lieutenants  taking their orders from their commander  or from the admiral , while a quartermaster  waited to carry them out to the ship.
k.t10-22-1: 22. — From that balcony the view is magnificent: it commands the whole beach with its tents  and bathing huts , and at bathing time one can see the bathers  frolicking merrily in front of the casino .
k.t10-23-1: 23. — At the end of the beach the coast forms a small rocky peninsula , where the breakers  come crashing in and on which a lighthouse  is built, showing sailors their way by night. This peninsula is joined to the land only by a very narrow isthmus .
k.t10-tit-8: A general view of the coast.
k.t10-24-1: 24. — The cliff  runs on, cut into by the sea, which carves out of it a whimsical series of bays  and headlands (capes), making it most picturesque.
k.t10-24-2: On the plateau  overlooking the strait  there is a very important fort  and a few villas.
k.t10-25-1: 25. — That strait separates from the mainland a very dangerous island , ringed with rocks  and reefs, where boats and even large ships are sometimes wrecked. For all the promptness of the rescue and the quick arrival of the lifeboats, these shipwrecks are terrible, and in the equinoctial gales several ships have been lost with all hands and cargo.
k.t10-25-2: In spite of that neighbourhood, the port is much used by sailors.
k.t11-apar-1: THIRD SERIES CHART No. 11 The Town and its buildings. — The Fire.
k.t11-c1-01-1: 1. — I live in a large town a hundred kilometres from the ocean, which is nevertheless a first-rate port (1). The river that runs along it is four hundred metres wide and forms a very fine roadstead.
k.t11-c1-02-1: 2. — The whole part of the town along the quays (2) has an entirely maritime and industrial look, and forms a suburb (3) lived in only by sailors and workers. The latter work in the factories (4) and at the gasworks (5), whose tall chimney (6) and gasholder can be seen from a long way off.
k.t11-c1-03-1: 3. — In the Middle Ages the town was fortified, and some remains of its ramparts can still be found, in particular the gate (8) of the old fortified castle (7) flanked by its two towers (9), which are now used as a prison.
k.t11-c1-04-1: 4. — In this whole quarter, which looks very old, only one building is comparatively modern: the customs house (10). It stands between the quay and the little street (11) leading to the old town hall (12). That last building is easy to recognise by the giant belfry (13) that towers over the old city.
k.t11-c1-05-1: 5. — On the other side of the street stands a building in the same style as the customs house: it is the exchange (14). One of its fronts looks on to a small square where the prefecture (15) is. Our town, in fact, without being a capital, is nevertheless an important county town.
k.t11-tit-2: The Upper Part of the Town.
k.t11-c1-06-1: 6. — The garrison, a fairly large one, is housed in vast and very healthy barracks (16); they stretch as far as the railings of the municipal park (17). The boulevard (19) leading to this park passes behind the savings bank (18) and comes out on the cathedral (20) square.
k.t11-c1-07-1: 7. — All these buildings rise in tiers on a small hill where our large secondary school (21) also stands.
k.t11-c1-07-2: If you go down a slightly sloping road that joins the High Street, you come to the law courts (22), in front of which lies a pleasant public garden (26). This square is not very large, but in the middle of the town it makes an oasis of greenery and cool air. So it is much frequented by the townspeople, who like to come and sit under the awning of the café (25) to listen to the military band that plays on Thursdays and Sundays in the bandstand (27) set among the lawns and flower beds.
k.t11-c1-08-1: 8. — On one of those lawns stands a bronze statue (28), a monument raised to the memory of one of our townsmen who rendered great service to the town of his birth.
k.t11-c1-09-1: 9. — Our town is not yet lit by electric light; it has only gas lamps (29). But the local press is campaigning for that system of lighting to be improved, just as the tramways’ system of traction has already been improved. The old carriages drawn by horses have been replaced by practical electric trams (31), which carry passengers quickly from one end of the town to the other at a very low fare.
k.t11-c1-10-1: 10. — Near the law courts is the bank (32), where commercial bills are discounted. The bank messengers (33) go round to people’s homes to collect what is owed.
k.t11-c1-11-1: 11. — The fine building close by is the museum. It houses at once the town library (34), some fine natural history collections (35) (a natural history museum) and a graceful picture gallery (36) that makes a splendid permanent exhibition.
k.t11-c1-11-2: It is open to the public twice a week, but visitors may see it any day for a small tip to the attendant (37). Painters (38) come to work there. You can see them in front of their easels, palette in hand, copying the famous pictures.
k.t11-c1-12-1: 12. — On the heights behind the museum you can just make out the dome (40) of the hospital (39) and the buildings of the teachers’ training college (41) where the teachers of our council schools were trained. On Theatre Square there is a post office (43) housed in a private house (42).
k.t11-tit-6: The Cry of Fire.
k.t11-c2-01-1: 1. — Alarming news is spreading through the town: fire has just broken out at the theatre! By the time I reach the square (96), the crowd has already gathered on the pavement (46) and on the roadway (47). The postal clerks (44) and the postmen (45) are coming out of the post office. A tram driver (48) has had to stop his tram to let through a municipal ambulance (50) arriving with a surgeon (52) and a nurse (51) to attend to an injured man (53) carried on a stretcher (54) to a spot near the newspaper kiosk (55).
k.t11-c2-02-1: 2. — A company of infantry on its way back from drill has stopped to help keep order with the mounted municipal guards (61). The horsemen, whose horses rear up, push back the onlookers (56) better than the soldiers (57) or the gendarmes (63) can. The gendarmes, besides, are very busy. One of them is telling the police officers (64) where to carry another casualty (65), a brave fireman who has fallen from a ladder.
k.t11-c2-03-1: 3. — The officer (66) points out exactly where the steam pump (67) now arriving must be placed. While waiting for that powerful machine, he has had a hand pump (68) set up, whose long hose (69) pours torrents of water on the fire. Six firemen are working it, while their comrade, holding the nozzle (70), aims the jet (71) at the heart of the blaze.
k.t11-c2-04-1: 4. — On the other side of the theatre the big ladder (72) has been raised. It lets the firemen get close to the flames leaping up amid swirls of black smoke (75).
k.t11-c2-05-1: 5. — The fire (74) started in the foyer of the theatre (73), during a rehearsal of the opera whose first performance was to have taken place tomorrow. Fortunately there were only a few spectators (76) in the auditorium. The poor people took refuge on the balcony (77), where brave firemen (86) are coming to their help with a ladder and ropes.
k.t11-c2-06-1: 6. — Under the portico (78), where the playbill (79) announces the performance, the musicians (81) of the orchestra (80) can be seen fleeing, carrying off their instruments: violin (81), flute (82), cello (83), trombone (84), drum (85), and so on. An effort is being made to save part of the furniture (87).
k.t11-c2-07-1: 7. — The actors (89) and actresses (88), singers both men and women, have had to run out in their stage costumes (90). The tenor is explaining to a journalist (92) how it happened. The reporter came running from the very first moment along with the authorities: the prefect (91), the mayor (93), the superintendent of police (94) and a magistrate (95), who will hold an inquiry to establish where the responsibility lies.
k.t12-apar-1: CHART No. 12 The Station. — The Railways. — The Boats. Note. — The timetables used in each country differ, so we have taken the times of the French chart as our example.
k.t12-01-1: 1. — I have just made a journey through Germany. Before setting out, I had bought a timetable  to find out the departure times of the trains. Having found that the most convenient train left Paris at nine in the evening and reached Strasbourg at one thirteen, I made ready for my journey, and the next day I had myself driven to the station.
k.t12-02-1: 2. — When I came into the great departure hall, behind an old country priest  carrying his travelling bag , a good many travellers  had already arrived.
k.t12-02-2: As I wanted to send a telegram , I had an inspector  point out the telegraph office  to me.
k.t12-03-1: 3. — Before going through to the waiting room , I went to get myself a return ticket .
k.t12-04-1: 4. — I did not wait long at the ticket window , for there were few people there. A soldier  going off on leave kindly gave me his turn, so that I had time enough to ask a few questions of the stationmaster , who was talking with the police superintendent  and the gendarme  on duty.
k.t12-05-1: 5. — After buying a paper at the bookstall , I had my luggage  weighed — a porter  had just brought it up on a luggage trolley . The clerk  in charge of the weighing machine  told me that my trunk weighed thirty-five kilograms, which made an excess of five kilograms, for which I had to pay a supplement at the luggage window .
k.t12-06-1: 6. — As I was early, I had time to watch the movement of travellers about the station. Some were leaving or collecting small bags at the left luggage office ; others were consulting the timetables . Arriving travellers hurried towards the exit  with their suitcases  in hand. A few waited at the luggage delivery  and handed over their ticket  to collect their trunks, crates  or baskets .
k.t12-07-1: 7. — The excise officers  went carefully through the parcels to see whether there was anything to declare.
k.t12-08-1: 8. — Some travellers made for the refreshment room , where a waiter  was busy serving them. They had to hurry, for the train , an express, would not stay long in the station.
k.t12-09-1: 9. — Then I went out on to the departure platform and looked for a through carriage  so as not to have to change during the journey. I got into a corridor coach with a compartment  for smokers and one reserved for “ladies travelling alone”.
k.t12-tit-2: Setting off by night.
k.t12-10-1: 10. — After climbing the step , shutting the door , rolling up the blind  and putting my small bags in the luggage rack , I sat down on the seat . Seeing the lamp man  light the lamps, I remembered that I had a night to spend in the carriage and called the attendant in charge of hiring out pillows  to ask him for one.
k.t12-11-1: 11. — The guard came to check the tickets. I asked him why we had not left, since it was the right time. He answered that the train chief  was busy having bicycles put in the luggage van . Besides, not all the foot warmers  had been changed yet.
k.t12-12-1: 12. — But we were soon to leave, for the fireman , up on his tender , was taking coal to stoke the fire of the locomotive , and the driver  was waiting only for the signal from the assistant stationmaster , who stood on the platform .
k.t12-13-1: 13. — The boiler  of the locomotive rumbled dully; the funnel  threw out torrents of smoke mixed with steam . A shrill whistle  rang out and the pistons  began to move, driving the wheels  of the heavy machine.
k.t12-14-1: 14. — The train, running on the rails , picked up speed; the platforms  came to an end; we passed the lavatories , and also a line of carriages standing on another track : sleeping cars , a restaurant car , a mail van .
k.t12-15-1: 15. — Then the goods station  passed before our eyes. Under the sheds, clerks were loading the goods  sent by slow train. Shunters  near the water tower  were moving cattle trucks  and flat wagons  to make up a goods train .
k.t12-16-1: 16. — We crossed the last points , beside which the signalman was standing; we passed the signal  and the station vanished into the distance.
k.t12-17-1: 17. — Soon we went out on to the iron bridge  that crosses the river . Once over the bridge, we ran along the river, on which powerful tugs  were pulling heavy barges . We also saw a passenger boat  just coming alongside a landing stage .
k.t12-18-1: 18. — After racing through several stations, we went through a few tunnels  and left behind us countless cottages  belonging to the crossing keepers. Rocked by the swaying of the train, I fell into a deep sleep.
k.t12-19-1: 19. — I was suddenly woken by the voice of an official shouting: “Deutsch-Avricourt! All change!” It was the customs inspection and all the tiresome formalities of the frontier. I had to set my watch by the station clock , which was fifty-five minutes fast; barely awake, I could hardly tell the big hand  from the little one ; the face  itself was quite blurred by the morning mist.
k.t12-20-1: 20. — While the customs officers went through their inspection, I yawned my way through the posters  that decorate the station walls. I had breakfast to pass the time, consulted the map of the German network  to see how far I still was from Strasbourg, and got back into my carriage, heartened by the hope of soon reaching my journey’s end.
k.t13-apar-1: CHART No. 13 The Hotel. — The Restaurant. The Café.
k.t13-01-1: 1. — Having arrived at Royan yesterday evening, I put up at the Ocean Hotel, which a friend had recommended to me.
k.t13-01-2: I was given a fine room  on the second floor , where I slept very well .
k.t13-02-1: 2. — This morning, on leaving my room, where the maid  had brought me my breakfast, I went into the smoking room , which also serves as a reading room , to look through the newspapers  while smoking a cigarette . When I had finished reading, I went down in the lift  and set off for a walk through the town.
k.t13-03-1: 3. — As I had forgotten to ask the hotel clerk  at what time meals were served at the table d’hôte , I came back early and took the chance to have a bath in the hotel bathroom . Then I went back to the cash desk  to telephone one of my friends. But the telephone  was engaged; seeing that I was at a loss, the cashier , who was entering a bill  in the guest register , asked the hall porter  to send the page boy  to run my errand on his bicycle .
k.t13-04-1: 4. — I thanked her and went out to tip the porter  (the odd-job man), who had brought from the station on his handcart  my hatbox , my suitcase  and my travelling bag . The postman , arriving just then, handed me a letter .
k.t13-05-1: 5. — I stayed a little longer on the doorstep, near the letterbox , watching the traffic in the street. The driver  of the omnibus  was loading on to his vehicle the trunk  of a guest  to whom the hotel keeper  was saying goodbye. A young telegraph boy  was bringing, in no hurry at all, a telegram  for one of the hotel’s guests; a tourist , with his camera  slung over his shoulder, was consulting his guidebook .
k.t13-06-1: 6. — In front of the railings, a placid errand man  was dozing between his carrying hooks  and his shoeshine box , while a young laundress  carrying a basket  of linen laughed at the solemn air of the head waiter  standing by the door.
k.t13-07-1: 7. — The sight of the cook , who had come out of his kitchen  in the basement  to send a kitchen boy  on an errand, reminded me that lunchtime was near, and I went to the restaurant across the yard, where a motorist  was parking his car  while a mechanic  repaired, following the directions of the cyclist , a motor tricycle  that had just had an accident.
k.t13-08-1: 8. — I asked a young groom  carrying glasses of beer  whether the table d’hôte was under the veranda, and on his saying that it was, I took a seat at one of the tables and had an excellent meal served to me.
k.t13-09-1: 9. — The waiter brought me the lunch menu and the wine list. I made my choice and ordered prawns with butter as a starter, and, for the first course, tripe Caen style. I had no fish, but asked for a portion of leg of lamb and, as a vegetable, creamed spinach. Then, as none of the sweet courses appealed to me, I had a variety of desserts brought: cheese, fruit and biscuits. I added an excellent Saint-Émilion wine, and, very pleased with my meal, I left the table after giving the waiter  a handsome tip .
k.t13-10-1: 10. — Seeing that I was ready to leave, the manager  suggested I step out on to the balcony to admire the splendid panorama of the ocean . In the distance one could make out small fishing boats , sailing ships  and an enormous liner  whose black silhouette stood out against the white clouds  on the horizon . A light breeze stirred the flag  planted above the sign  of the hall .
k.t13-11-1: 11. — The sight was so interesting that I decided to go up on to the café terrace the next day, taking with me a pair of opera glasses  or a telescope .
k.t13-12-1: 12. — On leaving the balcony I went to the hotel café for a drink  and a game of billiards . I walked straight through the café room, where many customers were playing chess , draughts , dominoes , backgammon  or cards , and went straight up to the billiard room .
k.t13-13-1: 13. — When the game was over, I went down to the ground floor and asked the waiter for an envelope , some paper , a postage stamp , a pen  and some ink  to write a letter.
k.t13-13-2: Then I called a coachman  whose carriage  had stopped in front of the café. I asked him his price by the hour and by the trip, and when we had agreed, he opened the carriage door  for me and settled me inside. He climbed back on to his seat , started the horses briskly with his whip , and off we went for a delightful drive.

noto.t01-noto-1: (*) For first names it is also recommended to transcribe them in their Latin form. That is the only way to avoid countless variants. Besides, how would one choose between Giovanni, Jean, Johann, Jan, Hans, John, Ivan, and so on? Are we to create a special dictionary of first names? Let us take the Latin nominative and say: Ioannes, Ioanna; Iulius, Iulia; Iakobus; Andreas; Lukas. (Complete Grammar).
noto.t02-noto-1: (*) Children’s games often have purely national names. We have named them in Ido as best we could, either by drawing on the very action that characterises them, or by adopting the national name of one country or another when it is not too misleading. For example: the barrel game (German and French) is the toad in the hole  (English), in which the players try to throw their round discs through the mouth of the metal toad that stands gaping on the pierced box (barrel). Shoulder-leap  differs from leapfrog only in this: to jump over the head, the players rest their hands on their partner’s shoulders, whereas in “leapfrog” they rest their hands only on his back. — Or again, some of the players bend over while the others vault over their backs with their hands on their shoulders; the first must take the shock without giving way, the second must jump without losing their balance (see the chart itself).
noto.t05-noto-1: (*) Balk-o = German Balken, English joist, French solive, Italian travicello, Russian balka, Spanish and Portuguese viga. A technical root not yet adopted, but proposed here to render the sense of the French word solive, which is neither a trabo (French poutre) nor a small beam. It is a squared timber that carries a floor and a ceiling.
noto.t06-noto-1: (*) Babo = a small child; English baby, French bébé, Italian bambino.
noto.t06-noto-2: (*) Lambrequino = French lambrequin, Spanish lambrequines, Portuguese lambrequins, and even German and English lambrequins — so German, English, French, Portuguese and Spanish alike.

noto.t08-noto-1: (*) Because this word is imprecise: is it a flax harvest, a grape harvest, an apple harvest? It might be better to use “ mesono ”, proposed in Mondo XIV, p. 242. But so far that new root has not been adopted by the Academy and awaits discussion under the usual rules of the Ido movement.
noto.t12-noto-1: (*) Note. — The journey is of course described as it was along the pre-war frontier.
noto.t13-noto-1: (*) For the details of the bedroom, see chart no. 6.
